name: Fuzz pedal enclosure
notes: Enclosure for a boutique guitar fuzz pedal, 125B-size. Top face: one 3PDT footswitch (12 mm hole) and two pots (7.5 mm holes). 1/4" input and output jacks on the long sides, 9 V DC jack on the top end. Four corner bosses take M3 screws for a flat bottom plate. It gets stomped on stage, so it must be tough, and the finish matters because boutique pedals sell on looks. Retail target around $180.

analysis.productSummary: A 125B-format boutique fuzz pedal shell: 122 x 66 x 39.5 mm open-bottom box, 2.5 mm walls, pre-punched for a 3PDT, two pots and three jacks. Sold to pedal players at ~$180, so it must survive stomping and look premium; at 250 units metal wins and tooling is unjustifiable.
detectedFeatures: Two 7.5 mm pot holes, top face
Two 1/4 inch jack holes on long sides
9 V DC jack hole on top end wall
Four corner bosses tapped for M3
Watertight mesh, no sub-1 mm walls

pros: Billet 6061 shell is the boutique-standard look and feel
Anodize or powder coat gives the premium finish buyers pay for
Six idle local mills; no tooling wait
Metal body shields pickups from hum
cons: Hogging out 36 mm of pocket is most of the cycle time
Side jack holes force a second and third fixture setup
Anodize color varies lot to lot

designTweaks.change: Match the interior profile to a stock 125B die-cast shell and CNC only the 12 mm, 7.5 mm and jack holes in a fixture.
designTweaks.why: Stock shells cost $5-8 and skip 20 minutes of pocket milling per part.
designTweaks.impact: Drops landed cost from ~$35 to ~$14/unit, bringing 250 units inside the $4,000 budget.

designTweaks.change: Move both 1/4 inch jacks and the DC jack to the top face alongside the footswitch, as most modern boutique pedals do.
designTweaks.why: All machined features then live on one face, so the part runs in one op on a vise or fixture plate.
designTweaks.impact: Removes two setups; roughly 20-25% lower unit cost and better pedalboard packing.

designTweaks.change: Give the 36 mm-deep cavity 6 mm corner radii and a flat floor, and tap M3 directly into solid 6 mm corner columns.
designTweaks.why: A 1/2 inch roughing endmill can then clear the pocket in few passes with no small-tool corner work.
designTweaks.impact: Cuts cycle time 25-35% and eliminates fragile cast-style bosses.

pros: Cheapest metal route that fits the $4,000 budget at 250
All holes cut in the flat blank by laser, no drilling
Five idle laser and three idle brake stations locally
Powder coat and screen print look genuinely boutique
cons: Folded 1.5 mm box is less rigid underfoot than billet
Corner welds need grinding before finish
Bosses must become PEM standoffs, extra hardware step
Hole positions shift slightly with bend tolerance

designTweaks.change: Redraw as one 1.5 mm 5052 blank with four bends and two welded end corners; replace the four M3 bosses with pressed-in standoffs.
designTweaks.why: A bend-and-weld box needs no pocket machining and uses the idle laser plus brake capacity.
designTweaks.impact: Unit cost roughly halves versus billet CNC, around $22 at 250 units.

designTweaks.change: Laser all five holes (12 mm, 2 x 7.5 mm, jacks) in the flat blank, keeping every hole at least 4 mm from any bend line.
designTweaks.why: Holes near a bend deform, and the 12 mm footswitch hole must stay round for the nut to seat.
designTweaks.impact: Eliminates a secondary drill op and scrap from distorted holes.

designTweaks.change: Add 3 mm corner relief notches and specify a 1.5 mm inside bend radius on all four walls.
designTweaks.why: Prevents tearing at the corners and makes the welded seams tight enough to grind flush.
designTweaks.impact: Cuts weld rework and lifts first-pass yield above 95%.

pros: No tooling and no fixtures; design changes are free
PA12 is genuinely tough and won't crack when stomped
122 mm part nests well in the 165 x 165 x 300 build
Can print PCB standoffs and cable guides for free
cons: Only two idle SLS machines locally; 250 units queues up
Grainy surface needs dye plus sealing for a boutique finish
Plastic body requires conductive shielding paint for hum
Cost never drops much below $25 at any volume

designTweaks.change: Thicken the top face to 4 mm within 15 mm of the 12 mm footswitch hole, blending back to 2.5 mm.
designTweaks.why: The stomp load concentrates at that hole and sintered nylon splits along layer lines there.
designTweaks.impact: Roughly doubles stomp life for about 3 g of extra powder.

designTweaks.change: Reduce the sidewalls from 2.5 mm to 2.0 mm and hollow the corner bosses to 3 mm wall around the M3 thread.
designTweaks.why: SLS is priced by volume and packed build height, and PA12 is stiff enough at 2 mm.
designTweaks.impact: ~15% less powder per part, about $4-6 off the unit price.

designTweaks.change: Print integral PCB standoffs and a DC-jack pocket into the cavity floor instead of using loose hardware.
designTweaks.why: Free geometry in SLS that would be expensive in any molded or machined version.
designTweaks.impact: Removes 4 fasteners and about 3 minutes of assembly per pedal.

pros: Cheapest part cost once past a few thousand units
PC/ABS survives stomping and takes texture well
Part fits comfortably in the 400 x 350 x 180 idle presses
Molded-in logo and texture cost nothing per shot
cons: Tooling is 3-5x the entire $4,000 budget at 250 units
Side jack holes need two slide actions, adding tool cost
Plastic needs shielding paint, adding $2-4 and a process step
Current model has no draft; requires CAD rework before quoting

designTweaks.change: Add 1.5 degrees of draft to all four interior walls of the 36 mm cavity and core the corner bosses to 2.5 mm wall.
designTweaks.why: Straight walls will drag and the solid bosses will sink-mark on a 2.5 mm nominal part.
designTweaks.impact: Enables a straight-pull core and removes visible sink on the show face.

designTweaks.change: Relocate both 1/4 inch jacks and the DC jack to the top face so no hole pierces a side wall.
designTweaks.why: Side holes each need a slide or hydraulic core in the tool.
designTweaks.impact: Cuts tooling from roughly $18k to $10k and shortens cycle time.

designTweaks.change: Support the footswitch hole with four 1.5 mm ribs underneath rather than thickening the top face.
designTweaks.why: Ribs add stiffness without the sink and long cooling time of a thick section.
designTweaks.impact: Keeps cycle near 35 s and avoids a cosmetic defect on the top face.

analysis.topRecommendation: For 250 units, buy stock 125B die-cast shells and have a local mill run only the hole pattern in a fixture, then powder coat: about $14-18 landed, inside your $4,000. If you want a full billet 6061 look, budget $8-12k instead. Injection molding only makes sense past roughly 3,000-4,000 units.
risks: Your $4,000 budget is $16/unit, which only the stock-shell-plus-machining route meets; full billet CNC runs 2-3x that.
The 36 mm interior depth is tight for a 3PDT plus wiring and a PCB, so mock up clearance before committing to 250 shells.
Two 7.5 mm pot holes in a 2.5 mm wall leave little thread engagement; check that standard 16 mm pot bushings and nuts seat.
Plastic paths (SLS or molded) need conductive shielding paint, adding cost and a hum risk boutique buyers will notice.
No photos or CAD with draft were supplied, so any injection-molding quote will require a model rebuild before it is valid.
